title: Decomposition and Reusable Components
learningObjectives: Describe the purpose of this function-related concept.
Identify its key parts or rules in an example.

Explain a common misuse and how to avoid it.
Apply the concept to a small programming task.

understand.concept: Decomposition means breaking a larger task into smaller, named parts that can be understood and tested. Reusable components are parts designed to serve more than one appropriate caller. A useful decomposition keeps each part focused and makes the whole workflow easier to follow without splitting everything into tiny fragments.
understand.whyItMatters: Large tasks become easier to reason about when each part has a clear responsibility. Reuse can reduce duplication, but overly generic components may obscure the real task.
understand.analogy: A team divides a delivery workflow into packing, labeling, and dispatch roles. The analogy is limited because software components may share data, call one another, or execute in different orders.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy omits language-specific implementation details; use it only as a first mental model.

explain.narrative: Start from the desired result, identify sub-tasks, give each one a clear boundary, and decide what information each sub-task needs. Reusable components should be stable and useful, not merely extracted because they are possible.

examples.explanation: A simple one-off expression may be clearer without an extra wrapper function.

examples.explanation: A focused component can be reused for multiple records.

commonMistakes: Splitting code into too many tiny pieces or overly broad components.
Ignoring inputs, outputs, or assumptions at boundaries.
Assuming runtime behavior is identical across languages.
Using abstraction or dependencies without a clear benefit.
